content: 1. Among individuals with tuberculosis (TB) and HIV co-infection, it is critical to evaluate the safety and tolerability of initiating antiretroviral therapy earlier, particularly in children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and those with drug-resistant TB. 2. Long-term safety and tolerability of newer antiretroviral drugs used in first-line, second-line, or third-line regimens in the context of TB and HIV co-infection must be assessed. 3. There is a need to address the data gap regarding the use of corticosteroids in preventing immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in people living with HIV who have low CD4 cell counts. 4. Longitudinal studies should be conducted to evaluate viral load suppression in individuals with HIV who are on efavirenz 400 mg formulations, especially in pregnant women and those receiving TB co-treatment, particularly when rifampicin is included in the TB treatment regimen. 5. The pharmacokinetics and safety of alternative dosing of tenofovir alafenamide when co-administered with TB treatment should be evaluated. 6. Health outcomes of individuals being treated for TB and histoplasmosis co-infection need to be measured. 7. The impact of macronutrient intake and food supplementation, in addition to TB treatment, on TB treatment outcomes should be measured. 8. The effects of macronutrient supplementation or routine micronutrient supplementation at recommended nutrient intake levels on pregnant women with active TB and neonatal complications should be studied. 9. The benefits of macroor micronutrient supplementation on the growth and development of young people aged 5–19 with active TB, compared to those without TB, should be assessed. 10. Nutritional parameters and TB-specific outcomes that can be measured in trials of nutritional supplementation need to be defined. 11. The effect of implementing WHO nutrition and TB recommendations on nutritional recovery and TB treatment outcomes should be measured. 12. The relative importance of food assistance compared to other enablers of adherence to TB treatment should be evaluated. 13. Aspects of nutritional counseling that enhance the effectiveness and uptake of advice on nutritional outcomes should be explored. 14. The best measure of nutritional status in pregnant women with and without TB, as well as maternal and infant outcomes, should be defined. 15. The optimal range of body mass index (BMI) for healthy maternal and infant outcomes in pregnant women with TB should be studied. 16. Energy requirements of TB patients and individuals without TB (including protein and fat requirements) should be assessed, considering TB treatment, coexistent HIV, treatment phase, and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). 17. The risk of micronutrient deficiencies in individuals with active TB compared to those without TB should be determined. 18. The proportional causes of malnutrition in individuals with TB should be explored. 19. The natural course of weight change during the intensive phase of TB treatment in individuals with drug-sensitive TB and MDR-TB, with varying degrees of malnutrition and in settings with different levels of food security, should be evaluated. 20. The relative risks for developing TB among non-injecting drug users, such as crack, cocaine, and opiate smokers, as well as people living with HIV and those who are HIV-negative, should be measured. 21. Confounders for TB disease risk among drug users, such as poverty, homelessness, and mental health problems, should be identified. 22. Country-specific contexts and risks for TB among drug users, particularly in India, Nepal, Pakistan, and other large Asian countries with high TB/HIV prevalence and growing injecting drug use, should be identified. 23. The overall impact of TB disease on drug users should be investigated. 24. Rates of MDR-TB and extensively drug-resistant TB among drug users should be characterized. 25. MDR-TB disease and treatment adherence among drug users inside and outside the prison system should be compared. 26. Specific barriers for women drug users to access TB care services in various settings, such as the criminal justice system, should be identified. 27. Effective and cost-effective strategies to promote adherence to TB treatment among drug users in low-income and resource-limited settings should be identified. 28. The overall impact of TB, TB/HIV, and drug use on the prison system should be assessed. 29. The frequency of reinfection during re-exposure among drug users in congregate settings, such as prisons and non-prison settings, and the implications on the cascade of care should be assessed. 30. Effective strategies for protecting healthcare workers and other personnel in healthcare and criminal justice settings from TB should be explored. 31. The most effective advocacy strategies for addressing TB among drug users should be identified. 32. The proportion of drug users who maintain treatment upon entry to prison and upon release or transfer should be assessed. 33. Strategies to limit loss-to-follow-up of drug users with TB who are released from prison while under TB treatment should be identified. 34. Best practices and strategies for caring for drug users with TB/HIV, other than in prisons, should be identified. 35. The proportion of TB detection and treatment outcomes among drug users in prisons should be determined. 36. In the context of the continuum of care, the best prison release practices for people who inject drugs and their relation to and integration with TB/HIV programs and services should be explored. 37. Current general practices for caring for terminally ill prisoners, such as incentives for discharge from prison, and whether mortality rates are monitored, should be mapped. 38. Research is essential for developing guidelines as it provides the evidence needed to address the wide-ranging problems faced by TB policymakers globally and nationally. 39. The WHO TB guidelines aim to stimulate large, well-funded, and well-coordinated research executed by skilled research teams in partnership with clinicians, patients, and policymakers, including WHO when possible. 40. Investment in TB research and development in 2021 was reported at $1 billion, far below the target of $5 billion per year set at the 2023 UN high-level meeting of the General Assembly. 41. To end TB by 2030, Member States must significantly increase their investment in TB research to ensure the development and uptake of new technologies and innovative approaches.
